Authors: NA
Title: Integrating multiple species connectivity and habitat quality into conservation planning for coral reefs
Taxa: 4 reef species: brooding coral, broadcasting coral, snapper, surgeonfish

Key_Finding: Dispersal barriers vary across species; no spatial concordance of high-quality sources, self-persistent, and stepping-stone reefs across species. Innovation: First integration of: (1) multiple species with different dispersal abilities, (2) habitat quality weighted connectivity metrics, (3) ecologically-informed parameters in Marxan for coral reef planning

Notes: Excellent methodological advancement for connectivity-informed MPA design. Directly addresses BRIDGES scope on spatial modeling for marine management.

Notes: Valuable for stakeholder integration in marine spatial planning. Social data methods transferable to coastal/marine contexts.

Title: Comparison of morphological and DNA metabarcoding analyses of diets in exploited marine fishes

Key_Finding: HTS (High-Throughput Sequencing) achieves similar taxon richness but significantly higher taxonomic resolution than microscopy. DNA barcode choice (COX1, 16S, 18S) affects resolution and phylogenetic breadth. HTS reveals previously unrecorded dietary items and parasite assemblages.
Innovation: First systematic comparison of morphological vs. DNA metabarcoding for parameterizing ecosystem models in fisheries context; demonstrates HTS potential for EBM
Limitations: Methodological comparison rather than model application; requires reference database development; semi-quantitative biomass estimates
Notes: Important methodological contribution for improving ecosystem model food web structure. Enables better EBM parameterization.

Innovation: Synthesizes disparate fisheries modeling approaches under single statistical framework; provides 4 worked examples with code; bridges theoretical statistics and practical fisheries applications
Limitations: Review/tutorial rather than applied study; computational demands for complex models; requires statistical expertise
Notes: Foundational statistical framework underpinning many modern fisheries spatial models. Essential methodological reference.

Title: Priority areas for biodiversity conservation in mainland Ecuador

Innovation: Integrates SDMs with Marxan for megadiverse country; combines biodiversity surrogates with climate adaptation criteria, ecosystem conversion risk, carbon, and accessibility layers

Notes: Exemplary national-scale conservation planning. Methods transferable to marine contexts. Climate adaptation integration valuable.

Authors: Howell D, Schueller AM, Bentley JW, Buchheister A, Chagaris D, Cieri M, Drew K, Lundy MG, Pedreschi D, Reid DG, Townsend H
Title: Combining Ecosystem and Single-Species Modeling to Provide Ecosystem-Based Fisheries Management Advice Within Current Management Systems
Spatial_Scope: US Atlantic (Atlantic menhaden); Irish Sea (multispecies fisheries)
Application: Direct TAC setting; ecological reference points for forage fish; ecosystem-informed quota advice within existing management frameworks
Key_Finding: Successful implementation in two management systems. For menhaden: ecological reference points account for predator needs. For Irish Sea: ecosystem variability influences quota setting within ICES PGY ranges. Both retain single-species model precision while adding ecosystem context.
Innovation: First operationalized framework combining ecosystem model strategic advice with single-species tactical advice for TAC setting. Introduces Feco concept - ecosystem-adjusted fishing mortality that stays within PGY ranges.
Limitations: Assumes ecosystem model correctly captures dynamics; F translation between models can be uncertain; requires both model types to be well-developed
Notes: Landmark paper for operational EBFM. Two independent case studies demonstrate generalizability.

Authors: Albouy C, Guilhaumon F, Leprieur F, Ben Rais Lasram F, Somot S, Aznar R, Velez L, Le Loc'h F, Mouillot D
Title: Projected climate change and the changing biogeography of coastal Mediterranean fishes
Application: Climate adaptation planning; MPA network design under climate change; fisheries adaptation strategies
Key_Finding: 1.4°C warming by mid-century, 2.8°C by end-century. 54 species lose climatically suitable habitat by 2099. Species richness decreases across 70.4% of continental shelf. Mean body size increases over 74.8% of shelf (loss of small species). Western Mediterranean and Aegean Sea most affected.
Innovation: First comprehensive ensemble SDM projection for Mediterranean coastal fish using regional climate model (NEMOMED8). Combines species richness and body size predictions.
Limitations: No dispersal constraints modeled; no biotic interactions; assumes niche conservatism; uncertainty in thermal tolerance
Notes: Highly influential for Mediterranean climate impact assessment. Founded subsequent work on functional/phylogenetic diversity impacts.

Authors: Ainsworth CH, Paris CB, Perlin N, Dornberger LN, Patterson WF III, Chancellor E, Murawski S, Hollander D, Daly K, Romero IC, Coleman F, Perryman H
Title: Impacts of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill evaluated using an end-to-end ecosystem model
Spatial_Scope: Gulf of Mexico (entire basin, 66 polygons, 7 depth layers)
Application: Oil spill damage assessment; ecosystem recovery planning; fisheries management post-disaster; closure evaluation
Key_Finding: Large reef fish biomass decreased 25-50% in most affected areas; large demersal fish decreased 40-70%. Recruitment effects and fishery closures had little influence compared to direct mortality/growth impacts. Missing generation of fish predicted. Recovery time decades for some guilds.
Innovation: First coupling of Lagrangian oil dispersion model with ATLANTIS ecosystem model. Dose-response relationships for fish mortality and growth from PAH exposure. Validated against independent ROV and tagging data.
Limitations: Uncertainty in oil concentration estimates; simplified dose-response; model complexity limits uncertainty quantification
Notes: Key paper from C-IMAGE consortium. Demonstrated ecosystem-scale oil spill impacts far beyond immediate spill zone.

Authors: Magris RA, Costa MDP, Ferreira CEL, Vilar CC, Joyeux JC, Creed JC, Copertino MS, Horta PA, Sumida PYG, Francini-Filho RB, Floeter SR
Title: A blueprint for securing Brazil's marine biodiversity and supporting the achievement of global conservation goals
Spatial_Scope: Brazil EEZ (Southwest Atlantic Ocean, ~3.5 million km²)
Application: National MPA network expansion; CBD Aichi Target 11 compliance; SDG 14 implementation; land-sea planning integration
Key_Finding: Industrial fisheries, climate change, and land-based activities are most severe threats. Systematic approach increases MPA coverage by only 7.9% compared to stakeholder proposals but with better biodiversity outcomes. Highest priorities in nearshore areas due to cumulative impacts.
Innovation: First comprehensive integration of cumulative impact assessment with Marxan for Brazil's EEZ. Combines representation, connectivity, and threat mitigation in single framework. Compares systematic priorities vs stakeholder-proposed MPAs.
Limitations: Data gaps in deeper waters; species distribution uncertainty; static threat assessment
Notes: Blueprint for Brazil's marine conservation. Strong policy relevance for expanding MPA network.

Authors: Alós J, Palmer M, Arlinghaus R
Title: Consistent Selection towards Low Activity Phenotypes When Catchability Depends on Encounters among Human Predators and Fish
Application: Understanding fishing-induced evolution; gear selectivity assessment; harvest control considering behavioral diversity
Key_Finding: Fishing consistently selects against high-activity phenotypes across all gear types tested. Selection differential strongest for passive gears (hooks, traps). Even short-term fishing can exert strong selection on behavioral traits. Home range size and activity are key determinants of vulnerability.
Innovation: First IBM explicitly linking individual fish behavior (activity, home range) to catchability through mechanistic encounter rates. Demonstrates fishing-induced selection on behavioral traits beyond body size.
Limitations: Simplified 2D movement; no social interactions; single species parameterization; no genetic component
Notes: Important for understanding non-size-selective fishing impacts. Foundational for fishing-induced evolution research.

Authors: Jennings S, Collingridge K
Title: Predicting Consumer Biomass, Size-Structure, Production, Catch Potential, Responses to Fishing and Associated Uncertainties in the World's Marine Ecosystems
Application: Global fisheries potential assessment; ecosystem-based reference points; climate-fisheries projections baseline
Key_Finding: Global consumer biomass (1g-1000kg): median 4.9 billion tonnes (90% CI: 0.3-26.1 billion tonnes). Uncertainty driven primarily by trophic transfer efficiency. ~77% of biomass in deep/offshore waters (visually misleading abundance near coasts). Fishing selectivity strongly affects sustainable yield estimates.
Innovation: First global-scale uncertainty quantification for marine consumer biomass using Monte Carlo parameter sampling. Couples simple macroecological model with dynamic size-trait model (mizer) for fishing impacts.
Limitations: Equilibrium assumption; no spatial dynamics; limited validation data; aggregate size classes
Notes: Key reference for global fish biomass estimates. Foundational for FishMIP model intercomparison.

Authors: Dubois M, Rossi V, Ser-Giacomi E, Arnaud-Haond S, López C, Hernández-García E
Title: Linking basin-scale connectivity, oceanography and population dynamics for the conservation and management of marine ecosystems
Application: MPA network design; genetic connectivity inference; population structure hypothesis generation; offshore reserve planning
Key_Finding: Retention weak in open ocean but significant in coastal areas. Wind-driven divergent regions = larval sources; convergent regions = larval sinks. Connectivity metrics (retention, betweenness, source/sink) are interrelated under specific conditions. Coastlines with sluggish circulation favor retention.
Innovation: First basin-scale systematic characterization of Mediterranean larval connectivity using network theory. Links retention/exchange metrics to oceanographic features (wind-driven divergence/convergence). Demonstrates interrelationship among connectivity metrics.
Limitations: Generic PLD (30 days); no larval behavior; no settlement habitat; validation limited to indirect evidence
Notes: Foundational for Mediterranean connectivity research. Framework for interpreting genetic patterns.

Authors: Rowden AA, Anderson OF, Georgian SE, Bowden DA, Clark MR, Pallentin A, Miller A
Title: High-Resolution Habitat Suitability Models for the Conservation and Management of Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems on the Louisville Seamount Chain, South Pacific Ocean
Spatial_Scope: Louisville Seamount Chain (SPRFMO Convention Area, South Pacific)
Application: SPRFMO bottom fishing spatial closures; VME protection; seamount management; fisheries impact assessment
Key_Finding: Abundance models outperform presence-absence models. Ensemble models have lower uncertainty. Suitable coral habitat concentrated at summit-slope breaks and along flanks ridges. Coral reef VME habitat occurs in small, isolated patches. Most seamount area unsuitable for VME.
Innovation: First high-resolution (25m) HSM for VME taxa on seamounts. Compares BRT, GAM, RF and ensemble approaches. Translates coral abundance thresholds to VME habitat definition. Within-seamount spatial closure feasibility assessment.
Limitations: Limited to surveyed seamounts; no substrate proxy; static predictions; orange roughy fishery context
Notes: Important for RFMO VME management. Demonstrates feasibility of within-seamount closures.

Authors: Nori J, Lescano JN, Illoldi-Rangel P, Frutos N, Cabrera MR, Leynaud GC
Title: Protected areas and spatial conservation priorities for endemic vertebrates of the Gran Chaco, one of the most threatened ecoregions of the world
Spatial_Scope: Gran Chaco ecoregion (Argentina, Paraguay, Bolivia ~1 million km²)
Application: Protected area expansion; conservation gap analysis; endemic species protection; land-use planning
Key_Finding: Current protected areas cover <15% of high-priority areas for endemics. Major conservation gaps in dry Chaco. Reptiles and amphibians most poorly represented. Priority areas concentrate in ecotones and highland refugia.
Innovation: First comprehensive spatial prioritization for Gran Chaco endemics. Combines SDMs with Zonation for systematic planning. Gap analysis of existing protected areas.
Limitations: Terrestrial focus (not marine); limited dispersal consideration; static climate baseline
Notes: Important for South American conservation. Terrestrial study but Zonation methodology relevant to marine applications.

Authors: Moullec F, Barrier N, Drira S, Guilhaumon F, Marsaleix P, Somot S, Ulses C, Velez L, Shin Y-J
Title: An End-to-End Model Reveals Losers and Winners in a Warming Mediterranean Sea
Application: Climate adaptation for Mediterranean fisheries; species-specific management strategies; ecosystem-based climate planning
Key_Finding: Total consumer biomass decreases 22% by 2099. Winners: small pelagics (anchovy, sardine), thermophilic species. Losers: demersal species, cold-water species, large predators. Western Mediterranean most impacted. Trophic amplification of climate impacts.
Innovation: First end-to-end (physics to fish) projection of Mediterranean marine ecosystems under climate change. Identifies species-specific winners and losers. Combines biogeochemical forcing with multispecies dynamics.
Limitations: RCP8.5 only; uncertain plankton responses; fishing held constant; no economic modeling
Notes: Key climate projection for Mediterranean fisheries. Identifies adaptation priorities.

Authors: Forney
Title: Habitat-based spatial models of cetacean density in the eastern Pacific Ocean
Spatial_Scope: Eastern Pacific Ocean (California Current Ecosystem + Eastern Tropical Pacific)
Taxa: 22 cetacean species/groups (blue whale, humpback, beaked whales, dolphins, porpoises)
Application: Environmental Impact Assessments; Navy sonar impact assessments; ship strike risk reduction; MPA planning; seasonal management zones
Key_Finding: Models successfully validated for 22 species. SST and MLD key predictors for most species. Blue whale density linked to productivity gradients. Beaked whales associated with deep water. Density predictions provide finer resolution than traditional line-transect estimates.
Innovation: First large-scale validated habitat-based density models for multiple cetacean species in Eastern Pacific. Combines line-transect distance sampling with GAM spatial modeling. Uses dynamic environmental covariates (SST, SSS, MLD, chlorophyll) for spatially explicit density predictions.
Limitations: Summer/fall surveys only; some species data-limited; model stationarity assumptions
Notes: Foundational paper for operational cetacean SDMs; enables quantitative impact assessment

Authors: Clay
Title: A comprehensive large-scale assessment of fisheries bycatch risk to threatened seabird populations
Spatial_Scope: Southern Ocean (circumpolar from South Georgia breeding populations)
Taxa: 4 threatened seabird species: Wandering albatross, Black-browed albatross, Grey-headed albatross, White-chinned petrel
Application: CCAMLR and RFMO bycatch mitigation; seabird conservation planning; fisheries management; Albatross Task Force priorities
Key_Finding: High spatial overlap between seabirds and fisheries in SW Atlantic, Indian Ocean sectors. Bycatch risk varies by life stage - non-breeders and immatures face highest exposure. Overlap regions correspond with documented high bycatch rates. Potential bycatch risk decreased since early 2000s but populations still declining.
Innovation: First comprehensive assessment integrating all life-history stages (breeding adults, non-breeders, immatures, juveniles) in bycatch risk analysis. Framework for population-weighted distributions from biologging data. Largest seabird tracking dataset used for risk assessment (1697 tracks, 790 individuals).
Limitations: South Georgia populations only; some fisheries underrepresented in AIS; temporal mismatch between tracking and effort data
Notes: Landmark paper for seabird-fisheries risk assessment; methodology now widely adopted

Authors: Atkinson
Title: KRILLBASE: a circumpolar database of Antarctic krill and salp numerical densities, 1926-2016
Spatial_Scope: Southern Ocean (circumpolar, south of Antarctic Polar Front)
Taxa: Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) and salps (Salpidae family)
Application: CCAMLR krill fishery management; ecosystem monitoring; climate change assessment; food web modeling; predator-prey dynamics
Key_Finding: Database contains 15,194 net hauls (12,758 krill, 9,726 salp records). Standardized values typically 2.2x raw values due to sampling corrections. Clear circumpolar distribution patterns with highest densities in Scotia Sea and WAP. Krill and salps show complementary distributions.
Innovation: First comprehensive circumpolar database of Antarctic krill and salp abundance. Data rescue and compilation from 10 nations. Standardization methodology corrects for sampling method differences (net type, time of day, season). Enables large-scale trend analysis and ecosystem modeling.
Limitations: Net sampling underestimates mobile krill; standardization has uncertainties; spatial coverage uneven; recent data bias
Notes: Essential resource for Southern Ocean ecosystem research; enables long-term trend analysis

Authors: Sinervo
Title: Erosion of Lizard Diversity by Climate Change and Altered Thermal Niches
Taxa: 48 Mexican Sceloporus lizard species; global lizard families
Application: Climate adaptation planning; extinction risk assessment; reserve design under climate change; prioritization of vulnerable species
Key_Finding: 12% of Mexican populations extinct since 1975. 4% of global populations extinct by 2009. Projected 39% local extinctions by 2080; 20% species extinctions. Viviparous species at higher risk (cannot shift breeding phenology). Model successfully hindcast extinctions on 4 continents.
Innovation: First global validated model linking thermal physiology to observed extinctions. Mechanistic approach using hours of restriction (hr) - time when environmental temperatures exceed activity thresholds. Validated predictions with actual documented local extinctions.
Limitations: Assumes no microhabitat buffering; limited dispersal consideration; behavioral plasticity underestimated
Notes: Landmark paper demonstrating climate-driven extinctions are already occurring; highly cited

Authors: Bode
Title: Successful validation of a larval dispersal model using genetic parentage data
Spatial_Scope: Great Barrier Reef (3 reef clusters, 60-220 km separation)
Temporal_Scope: Multi-year simulations validated against 2007-2014 genetic data
Taxa: Coral reef fish (Plectropomus maculatus and P. leopardus - coral trout/groupers)
Application: MPA network design validation; connectivity assessment; reserve spacing optimization; fisheries replenishment
Key_Finding: Validated model predicts consistent connectivity patterns with genetic parentage assignments. Models slightly overpredict short-distance dispersal. Median dispersal distances ~110-190 km. Long-distance dispersal (up to 250 km) confirmed by both model and genetics.
Innovation: First successful validation of biophysical larval dispersal model using genetic parentage data. Demonstrates that properly parameterized models can accurately predict larval connectivity. Provides methodology for model validation essential for MPA design.
Limitations: Relies on intensive genetic sampling; species-specific; validation limited to two grouper species
Notes: Critical proof that biophysical models can be trusted for MPA design decisions

Authors: Limburg
Title: Ocean Deoxygenation: A Primer
Temporal_Scope: Mid-20th century to present + future projections
Taxa: Marine ecosystems generally; fish and invertebrates specifically affected
Application: Climate mitigation policy; nutrient reduction strategies; fisheries adaptation; coastal zone management; ecosystem-based management
Key_Finding: 1-2% global ocean O2 inventory lost since mid-20th century. >700 coastal sites with new/worsening low O2. Climate warming reduces O2 solubility and ventilation. Eutrophication drives coastal hypoxia. Impacts include habitat compression, reduced growth, reproductive impairment, disease susceptibility.
Innovation: First comprehensive accessible primer on ocean deoxygenation for broad audience. Synthesizes mechanisms (climate warming, eutrophication), scale (1-2% global O2 loss, 700+ coastal dead zones), and impacts (individual to ecosystem level). Integrates human well-being impacts.
Limitations: Review not primary research; limited quantitative projections; regional variation not fully captured
Notes: Excellent accessible introduction to deoxygenation; valuable for non-specialists

Authors: Brooks
Title: Factors controlling the seasonal distribution of pelagic Sargassum
Spatial_Scope: North Atlantic (tropical Atlantic, Sargasso Sea, Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean)
Taxa: Pelagic Sargassum (S. fluitans and S. natans)
Application: Sargassum beaching prediction; Caribbean coastal management; tourism sector planning; ecosystem monitoring
Key_Finding: Passive advection alone explains only 60% of distribution during some periods. Adding growth, mortality, fragmentation achieves 65-75% accuracy. Sargasso Sea acts as 'dead end' for Sargassum. Gulf of Mexico and Western Tropical Atlantic disproportionately influence basin biomass. Tropical Atlantic population new since 2011.
Innovation: First coupled modeling approach integrating ocean circulation with Sargassum physiology to explain seasonal distributions. Demonstrates that advection alone is insufficient - growth, mortality, and fragmentation essential for realistic predictions. Proposes conceptual seasonal cycle model.
Limitations: Simplified physiology; single morphotype; uncertain fragmentation rates; limited validation data pre-2011
Notes: Foundational for understanding Sargassum blooms causing Caribbean inundations since 2011

Authors: Flórez
Title: Defensive symbiosis: a microbial perspective
Taxa: Symbiotic microbes providing chemical defense to hosts (insects, marine invertebrates, plants)
Application: Limited direct spatial modeling relevance; useful for understanding ecosystem function and bioactive compound discovery
Key_Finding: Defensive symbionts widespread across metazoan phyla. Chemical compounds often novel natural products. Symbionts can be vertically or horizontally transmitted. Defense effectiveness context-dependent. Symbiosis can drive host diversification.
Innovation: Synthesizes defensive symbiosis across terrestrial and marine systems from microbial perspective. Identifies common themes in chemical defense production, ecological contexts, and evolutionary implications.
Limitations: Not a spatial model; limited quantitative application; primarily terrestrial focus
Notes: Out of scope for BRIDGES spatial modeling focus - may be false positive in database

Authors: Jones
Title: Predicting the Impact of Climate Change on Threatened Species in UK Waters
Taxa: 7 threatened marine species (skates, rays) + 10 commercial demersal fish species
Application: MPA effectiveness assessment under climate change; threatened species conservation; bycatch risk mitigation; UK marine spatial planning
Key_Finding: Species projected to shift northward at ~27 km/decade average. Critically Endangered D. batis may gain 40% suitable habitat if able to disperse. R. alba faces increased bycatch risk due to increased overlap with commercial species. Protected areas show variable future suitability - some improve, others decline.
Innovation: First multi-model ensemble SDM approach for threatened marine vertebrates in UK waters. Combines three SDMs with two climate projections (GFDL, CMIP3). Assesses protected area effectiveness under climate change. Calculates bycatch risk through range overlap between commercial and threatened species.
Limitations: Single region (UK); limited dispersal modeling; 2050 horizon only; assumes static protected areas
Notes: Important for UK marine conservation planning; demonstrates multi-model ensemble value

Authors: Schulp
Title: Use of demand for and spatial flow of ecosystem services to identify priority areas
Taxa: Ecosystem services (carbon, flood regulation, air quality, pollination, urban leisure)
Application: EU land use planning; Natura 2000 network evaluation; green infrastructure planning; ES conservation priority setting
Key_Finding: Only 37.1% overlap between priority areas with/without demand accounting. Ignoring ES demand leads to conservation priorities in remote areas with little human benefit. Flow zone approaches enhance ES distribution without major trade-offs. Global ES (carbon) less affected than local ES by demand consideration.
Innovation: First integration of ES demand and flow zones into spatial prioritization using Zonation. Tests multiple approaches to account for supply-demand connections. Demonstrates that ignoring demand leads to priority areas in remote regions with low societal benefit.
Limitations: Terrestrial focus (not marine); static ES maps; simplified flow models
Notes: Primarily terrestrial but methodology applicable to marine ES; valuable for coastal/marine ES planning

Authors: Shenton
Title: Bayesian network models for environmental flow decision-making: 1. Latrobe River Australia
Taxa: Australian Grayling (Prototroctes maraena) and River Blackfish (Gadopsis marmoratus)
Application: Environmental flow allocation; dam release optimization; water sharing plans; fisheries conservation
Key_Finding: BN successfully integrates expert knowledge with available data. Identifies critical flow requirements for spawning and juvenile recruitment. Provides probabilistic predictions of fish population outcomes under different flow scenarios. Demonstrates transparency in decision-making process.
Innovation: First application of BN for transparent environmental flow decision-making with explicit uncertainty handling. Links flow regimes to fish life history stages. Provides probability distributions for management outcomes rather than point estimates.
Limitations: Freshwater focus; data-limited system requires expert opinion; single river system
Notes: Freshwater system but methodology highly transferable to coastal/estuarine systems

Authors: Brooks
Title: Competing values on the Antarctic high seas: CCAMLR and the challenge of marine-protected areas
Taxa: Antarctic krill and toothfish fisheries; broader MPA network
Application: CCAMLR MPA policy; high seas governance; international conservation negotiation strategy
Key_Finding: Number of CCAMLR fishing States increased 4-fold since 1982. Toothfish brings 20x more profit than krill despite lower catch. Ross Sea and East Antarctic MPA proposals stalled due to fishing State objections. Russian delegation questioned CCAMLR's legal authority for MPAs.
Innovation: Comprehensive policy analysis of barriers to Southern Ocean MPA adoption. Documents the rise of toothfish fishing interests as obstacle to conservation. First detailed examination of CCAMLR MPA negotiation process.
Limitations: Not a spatial modeling study; policy focus rather than technical
Notes: Important context for CCAMLR spatial planning but not a modeling study per se

Authors: Trites
Title: Ecosystem Change and the Decline of Marine Mammals in the Eastern Bering Sea: Testing the Ecosystem Shift and Commercial Whaling Hypotheses
Taxa: Marine mammals (seals, sea lions, whales); pollock; large flatfish; entire food web
Application: Bering Sea fisheries management; marine mammal recovery planning; ecosystem-based management
Key_Finding: Pollock contributed >50% of mid-trophic energy flow in 1980s vs 10% in 1950s. Large flatfish and pollock are significant seal competitors. Marine mammal biomass changes have little effect on other groups. Ecosystem more mature in 1950s. Whale removal had positive effect on pollock through reduced competition.
Innovation: Tests competing hypotheses for marine mammal declines using comparative EwE models. Examines ecosystem shift vs whaling removal hypotheses. Quantifies energy flow changes across decades.
Limitations: 1950s data uncertainty; static snapshots; limited spatial resolution
Notes: Important for understanding ecosystem-level impacts of fishing and environmental change

Authors: Olsen
Title: Ecosystem Model Skill Assessment. Yes We Can!
Taxa: Multiple species (fish biomass, landings, ecosystem indicators)
Application: Ecosystem model validation protocols; management strategy evaluation; model credibility assessment
Key_Finding: NEUS Atlantis model performs above average for key species. Forecast skill comparable to hindcast skill - critical for management use. Multiple metrics essential for comprehensive assessment. Framework applicable to any predictive model.
Innovation: First comprehensive skill assessment of a full marine ecosystem model. Develops best-practice framework using multiple metrics (RMSE, AAE, MEF, correlation). Demonstrates 10-year forecast skill comparable to hindcast skill.
Limitations: Single model/region tested; skill varies by species
Notes: Essential reading for anyone using ecosystem models for management

Authors: Gilles
Title: Seasonal habitat-based density models for a marine top predator, the harbor porpoise, in a dynamic environment
Spatial_Scope: Central and Southern North Sea (UK, Belgium, Netherlands, Germany, Denmark)
Application: EU Habitats Directive assessment; Marine Strategy Framework Directive; offshore wind farm impact assessment; MPA designation
Key_Finding: Models capture seasonal distribution shifts across international boundaries. Depth, distance to shore, distance to sandeel grounds, SST, and fronts are key predictors. Day length proved good proxy for seasonal variation. Southern North Sea shows increasing importance.
Innovation: First international compilation of porpoise survey data for seasonal SDM across North Sea. Combines SCANS-II with national surveys (156,630 km, 14,356 sightings). Uses day length and SST as season proxies for space-time predictions.
Limitations: Summer bias in some years; visual surveys only; surface availability
Notes: Exemplary international collaboration; operational for North Sea spatial planning

Authors: Schill
Title: No Reef Is an Island: Integrating Coral Reef Connectivity Data into the Design of Regional-Scale Marine Protected Area Networks
Spatial_Scope: Caribbean Basin and Gulf of Mexico (10 marine ecoregions)
Application: Caribbean-wide MPA network design; transboundary reef conservation; reef resilience planning; Haiti-DR-Cuba corridor
Key_Finding: 77% of high-connectivity reefs not in existing MPA network. Mesoamerican Reef, Bahamas, and Cuba are key connectivity corridors. Eastern Caribbean small island reefs vulnerable to isolation. Network graph metrics (betweenness, closeness centrality) identify keystone reefs.
Innovation: First Caribbean-wide integration of larval connectivity into Marxan MPA design. Quantifies connectivity by EEZ for transboundary planning. Uses asymmetric boundary files based on larval flow rather than Euclidean distance. 4-year multi-spawn synthesis.
Limitations: Coral focus only; 30-day PLD assumption; no genetic validation
Notes: Landmark paper for regional marine connectivity-based conservation planning

Authors: Zorrilla
Title: Evaluation of Bayesian Networks in Participatory Water Resources Management, Upper Guadiana Basin, Spain
Application: EU Water Framework Directive implementation; groundwater management; stakeholder conflict resolution
Key_Finding: BN effective for structuring stakeholder discussions. Visual appeal aids communication across groups. Participatory process enhanced understanding of trade-offs. Farmers, authorities, and environmentalists achieved shared understanding.
Innovation: Develops and tests evaluation criteria for participatory BN modeling. Documents stakeholder engagement process for water conflicts. Provides framework for assessing participatory modeling quality.
Limitations: Freshwater/terrestrial focus; single case study; qualitative evaluation
Notes: Freshwater focus but participatory approach valuable for marine stakeholder engagement

Authors: Plecha
Title: Global marine heatwave events using the new CMIP6 multi-model ensemble: from shortcomings in present climate to future projections
Temporal_Scope: Historical (1971-2014); Future (2041-2100) under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5
Application: Climate adaptation planning; marine ecosystem risk assessment; fisheries management under climate change
Key_Finding: MME underestimates observed frequency by 21% and intensity by 31%, overestimates duration by 100%. Future MHWs approach near-permanent state by end-century under high emissions. Intensity increases 0.2-1.5°C depending on pathway. CMIP6 biases similar to CMIP5 - high-resolution models still needed.
Innovation: First comprehensive CMIP6 MHW assessment. Validates 12 GCMs against NOAA OISST observations. Provides future projections under three emission scenarios. Identifies persistent GCM biases in MHW properties.
Limitations: Coarse resolution; known GCM biases; no ecosystem coupling
Notes: Essential baseline for marine ecosystem climate impact assessment

Innovation: Novel Marxan adaptation for river systems accounting for longitudinal connectivity, basin divides, and upstream threat propagation; critical management zones (riparian buffers, migration corridors)

Notes: Landmark paper for freshwater Marxan applications. Methods for connectivity and threat propagation highly relevant to marine spatial planning. Network covered 11% of study area.

Title: Merging connectivity rules and large‐scale condition assessment improves conservation adequacy in river systems
Drivers: River condition, upstream impacts, connectivity requirements
Application: Conservation adequacy in freshwater; accounts for natural decay of upstream influences with distance; whole sub-basin vs corridor prioritization
Innovation: Novel 'virtual boundaries' and distance-weighted penalties for upstream connectivity; connectivity strength modifier (CSM) calibration; merges connectivity rules with condition assessment
Limitations: Freshwater focus; requires detailed stream network data
Notes: Important methodological advance for connectivity in systematic conservation planning. The virtual boundaries and distance-weighted penalties could be adapted for larval connectivity in marine systems.

Spatial_Scope: Greater Virunga Landscape (DRC, Uganda, Rwanda - Africa)
Taxa: Large mammals (mountain gorillas, elephants), landscape species
Drivers: Threat distribution (poaching), patrol costs, species distributions
Application: Ranger patrol optimization; anti-poaching; 63% cost reduction while meeting conservation targets; patrol costs $2.2-3.5M vs $6.5M for full coverage
Innovation: Novel Marxan application for law enforcement allocation; threat mapping combined with conservation targets; cost-efficiency analysis of patrol posts vs mobile patrols
Limitations: Terrestrial context; assumes static threat distribution
Notes: Innovative extension of Marxan beyond reserve design to operational management. The patrol optimization approach is directly applicable to marine protected areas for enforcement targeting.

Authors: Lessmann J, Fajardo J, Muñoz J, Bonaccorso E
Title: Large expansion of oil industry in the Ecuadorian Amazon: biodiversity vulnerability and conservation alternatives
Taxa: 745 species (amphibians, birds, butterflies, mammals, plants); 25 ecosystems
Drivers: Oil block expansion, deforestation, habitat loss
Application: Conservation planning under development pressure; 68% of Amazon in oil blocks; southern Amazon identified as priority; scenarios achieving 38-85% coverage
Innovation: Scenario analysis comparing conservation options under oil expansion; oil block importance index combining species diversity, ecosystem diversity, natural vegetation, priority areas
Limitations: Terrestrial Amazon; SDM bias from museum specimens; static threat assessment
Notes: Demonstrates Marxan use for development-conservation tradeoffs. Relevant to marine contexts where oil/gas development threatens biodiversity (e.g., Arctic, deep-sea).

Authors: Christensen V, Coll M, Buszowski J, Cheung WWL, Frölicher T, Steenbeek J, Stock CA, Watson RA, Walters CJ
Title: The global ocean is an ecosystem: simulating marine life and fisheries
Taxa: Primary producers to top predators; commercial fish stocks; 60 functional groups
Drivers: SST, NPP, oxygen, fishing effort by fleet and gear type
Application: Global fisheries management; climate change impact assessment; evaluation of alternative management scenarios on seafood supply
Innovation: First spatially-explicit global marine food web model; integrates biogeochemical forcing (NPP) with fisheries dynamics; Markov chain stock reduction analysis for calibration
Limitations: Coarse resolution for local management; functional group aggregation; calibration challenges
Notes: Landmark paper establishing EcoOcean as global marine ecosystem model. Enables scenario testing of fisheries management and climate change at global scale. Most detailed global fisheries model ever constructed.

Title: Defining trends and thresholds in responses of ecological indicators to fishing and environmental pressures
Spatial_Scope: Northeast Shelf Large Marine Ecosystem (USA, Cape Hatteras to Nova Scotia)
Drivers: AMO (Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation), SST, fishing pressure (landings)
Application: Ecosystem-based fisheries management (EBFM); reference point development; identifying critical pressure values
Innovation: Empirical determination of numerical thresholds where fishing and environmental pressures significantly alter ecological indicators; non-linear GAM relationships
Limitations: Correlative relationships; assumes stationarity in ecological processes
Notes: Important methodological contribution for identifying ecosystem thresholds. Directly supports EBFM implementation by providing quantitative pressure-response relationships.

Authors: Christensen V, de la Puente S, Sueiro JC, Steenbeek J, Majluf P
Title: Valuing seafood: The Peruvian fisheries sector
Taxa: Anchoveta (Engraulis ringens), all commercial species, 35 enterprise types
Drivers: Fleet economics, processing pathways, market destinations
Application: Fisheries policy; demonstrates human consumption generates 2x revenue and 3x jobs vs fishmeal production; economic multipliers ~2.9 across industry
Innovation: Novel ecosystem-economic modeling integrating EwE with comprehensive value chain analysis; first full sector valuation showing anchoveta is only 31% of GDP despite dominating catches
Limitations: Single year snapshot; assumes market conditions stable
Notes: Demonstrates that directing fish to human consumption rather than fishmeal/oil creates more economic and social benefit. Challenges dominant fishmeal industry narrative. 35% of jobs in restaurants.

Authors: de Mutsert K, Steenbeek J, Lewis K, Buszowski J, Cowan JH Jr, Christensen V
Title: Exploring effects of hypoxia on fish and fisheries in the northern Gulf of Mexico using a dynamic spatially explicit ecosystem model

Application: Gulf hypoxia management; fisheries impact assessment; Mississippi River nutrient reduction scenarios
Innovation: Novel Ecospace plug-in for spatially-temporally dynamic DO and Chl-a forcing from coupled ROMS-biogeochemical model; separates positive (bottom-up fueling) and negative (hypoxia) effects of nutrients
Limitations: Model parameterization for DO response; functional group aggregation
Notes: Demonstrates that nutrient-driven productivity increases outweigh hypoxia decreases at aggregate level, BUT species-specific responses vary (red snapper net loss). Critical for nutrient management policy.

Title: Trans-Amazonian natal homing in giant catfish
Application: Fisheries connectivity; Dam impact assessment; International transboundary management; Migration corridor protection
Innovation: First confirmation of long-distance natal homing in freshwater fish (8000+ km round trip); Otolith 87Sr/86Sr microchemistry to track individual movements; Demonstrates compulsory migratory lifecycle
Limitations: Not a spatial prediction model; Focused on single species; Indirect spatial inference
Notes: Methodologically important for connectivity but not spatial modeling per se; Highly relevant for dam impact assessment

Authors: Renaud
Title: Pelagic food-webs in a changing Arctic: a trait-based perspective suggests a mode of resilience
Taxa: Calanus copepod complex (C. glacialis, C. hyperboreus, C. finmarchicus)
Drivers: Climate change, sea ice loss, primary production regimes, temperature
Application: Arctic fisheries management; Climate change adaptation; Food web resilience assessment
Innovation: Trait-based perspective on Calanus species shifts; Challenges assumption that smaller boreal species replacing Arctic species will harm predators; Suggests energy transfer efficiency may compensate for body size changes
Limitations: Conceptual/review rather than quantitative spatial model; Limited empirical validation
Notes: Important conceptual framework for Arctic; Trait-based approach highly relevant but not spatially explicit

Authors: Hollowed
Title: Integrated Modeling to Evaluate Climate Change Impacts on Coupled Social-Ecological Systems in Alaska
Taxa: Commercial fish and shellfish (walleye pollock, Pacific cod, crab)
Drivers: Climate scenarios (CMIP5), oceanography (ROMS), biogeochemistry, fishing pressure
Application: NPFMC decision support; Climate-ready fisheries management; Management strategy evaluation; Ecosystem approach to fisheries management
Innovation: LANDMARK: Multi-model ensemble approach for climate-fisheries projections; Integrates GCMs, regional ocean models, population dynamics, economics, and MSE; Uncertainty decomposition (scenario, parameter, structural); 5-year iterative cycle matching stock assessment cycle
Limitations: EBS-specific parameterization; Computationally intensive; Requires substantial data infrastructure
Notes: LANDMARK PAPER - Best practice for integrated climate-fisheries modeling; Direct management application

Authors: Amandè
Title: Precision in bycatch estimates: the case of tuna purse-seine fisheries in the Indian Ocean
Taxa: Bycatch species (sharks, rays, billfish, sea turtles, small tunas)
Drivers: Fishing mode (FAD vs free school), observer coverage
Application: Observer program design; Bycatch estimation precision; RFMO compliance monitoring
Innovation: Quantifies relationship between observer coverage and bycatch estimate precision; Shows 4.6% coverage yields >50% RRMSE for all species; GLM explains 85% of variability in estimate precision; Identifies minimum coverage requirements
Limitations: Focused on precision not accuracy; Does not address observer behavior biases; Species-specific coverage needs vary widely
Notes: Important for fisheries monitoring design; Statistical methods broadly applicable

Authors: O'Brien
Title: A regional-scale ecological risk framework for environmental flow evaluations
Spatial_Scope: Senqu River (Lesotho/South Africa) and Mara River (Kenya/Tanzania)
Taxa: Fish communities, riparian vegetation, aquatic invertebrates
Drivers: Flow alterations, dam barriers, water abstraction
Application: Environmental flow assessment; Dam impact evaluation; Ecosystem services risk assessment; Water resource development planning
Innovation: Regional-scale BN framework integrating ecological endpoints with socio-economic services; Spatially-referenced source-stressor-receptor pathways; Applicable to transboundary water management
Limitations: Freshwater focus; Requires expert knowledge for BN parameterization; Relative rather than absolute risk
Notes: Freshwater focus but methods applicable to estuarine/coastal systems; BN approach valuable for integrated risk assessment

Authors: Sundblad
Title: Ecological coherence of marine protected area networks: a spatial assessment using species distribution models
Taxa: Coastal fish species (perch, pike) and habitat-forming species
Application: MPA network design; Natura 2000 assessment; Ecological coherence evaluation (adequacy, representativity, replication, connectivity)
Innovation: SDM-based framework for assessing MPA network ecological coherence; Quantifies four coherence criteria; Identifies gaps in existing Natura 2000 network; Species-specific connectivity requirements
Limitations: Static assessment (no temporal dynamics); Connectivity assessment limited by dispersal knowledge; Baltic-specific validation
Notes: Important for MPA network assessment; SDM methods widely applicable

Authors: Kaplan
Title: Fishing catch shares in the face of global change: a framework for integrating cumulative impacts and single species management
Journal: Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences
Taxa: Groundfish (English sole, arrowtooth flounder, yellowtail rockfish, bocaccio)
Drivers: Ocean acidification (pH decline), fishing pressure (IFQ scenarios)
Application: IFQ/catch share design; Climate-robust fisheries management; Cumulative impact assessment; MSE
Innovation: First integration of ocean acidification with fisheries catch share scenarios in Atlantis; Shows indirect food web effects (prey loss) dominate over direct fishing effects; Demonstrates need for climate-robust management designs
Limitations: Acidification impacts on benthos uncertain; Limited empirical validation of pH effects; Single system application
Notes: Important early application of Atlantis for climate + fisheries integration; Framework remains highly relevant
